title: How does HTTPS work

segments.text: Hi, welcome to another byte-by-go system design video. In this video, we'll talk about HTTPS.
What is so important about HTTPS at these days, most websites require it. How does HTTPS work?
We'll answer these questions in this video. Let's dive right in.
Without HTTPS, the communication between the browser and the server is in plain text.
This means that the password you enter or the credit card number you sent over in and that,
can be read by anyone who has the ability to intercept it.
HTTPS is designed to solve this problem,
to make the data send over in and that unreadable by anyone other than the sender and the receiver.
HTTPS is an extension of the HTTP protocol.
We discussed HTTPS in our last video. Check the link down below if you like to learn more about it.
With HTTPS, data is sending an encrypted form using something called TLS.
TLS stands for transport layer security.
If the encrypted data gets intercepted by a hacker, all they could see is jumbo data.
This is where TLS handshake comes in. Let's take a look at how this handshake works.
There are several steps. Step 1. Just like the case with HTTPS, the browser establishes a TCP connection with the server.
Step 2. This is where the TLS handshake begins.
The browser sends a client hello to the server. In this hollow message, the browser tells the server the following things.
1. What TLS versions it can support it could be TLS 1.2 TLS 1.3 so on and so forth.
2. What cybersecurity supports a cybersecurity is a set of encryption algorithms to use to encrypt data.
After receiving the client hello, the server gets to choose the cybersecurity and the TLS version to use.
Based on the options it got from the client.
It sends those in a server hollow message back to the client.
The server then sends a certificate to the client. The certificate includes a lot of different things.
One of the key things is the public key for the server.
The client uses the public key in something called asymmetric encryption.
In asymmetric encryption, a piece of data that is encrypted by a public key can only be decrypted by the private key.
We'll discuss how this is used in a bit. This concludes Step 2. The hollow face of the TLS handshake.
At this point, the client has a server certificate and the client and a server have agreed on the TLS version and the cybersecurity to use.
Now to step 3. This is to step work the client and the server come up with a share encryption key to use to encrypt data.
This is the puzzle we talked about earlier.
And this is what asymmetric encryption comes into picture.
Again, with asymmetric encryption, the data encrypted on the client side using the public key from the server can only be decrypted by the server.
This is how the client sends an encryption key safely to the server over the wide open internet.
All this is done in the client key exchange message.
This exact detail varies depending on the surface we used.
Here we use RSA as an example since it is an easiest to understand.
With RSA, the client generates an encryption key, also call a session key,
and encrypts it with the server's public key and sends the encrypted session key to the server over the internet.
The server receives the encrypted session key and decrypts it with this private key.
So now the server has the session key too.
Now both sides hold the session key and this is where the intercept four of the TLS handshake.
Where they use the session key and agree upon Cypher Suite to send encrypted data back and forth in a secure bi-directional channel.
Now you might ask, why don't we just use asymmetric encryption for everything?
Why switch to a symmetric encryption at all?
The main reason is that asymmetric encryption is computationally expensive.
This is something suitable for bulk data transmission.
Now before we close, there are two finer points I would like to discuss.
First, the handshake we talked about applied to TLS 1.2.
While the latest version of TLS is 1.3, and 1.3 is supported on all major browsers.
As we can see in our illustration, TLS 1.2 takes two n° trips to complete.
This is one of the major improvements of TLS 1.3.
It optimizes the handshake to reduce a number of n° trip to 1.
We decided to talk about TLS 1.2 because we reviewed TLS 1.3 as an optimization.
As with most optimizations, it is a bit harder to explain.
This one we chose TLS 1.2 instead.
The core concept in TLS 1.2 still applied to 1.3.
The second finer point we would like to discuss is that in the explanation about we used RSA for asymmetric encryption
to securely exchange the symmetric session key.
Again, we chose RSA because it is easy to understand.
However, asymmetric encryption is not the only way to share the session key between the client and the server.
In fact, the TLS 1.3 RSA is no longer supported as a method for key exchange.
Tiffy Helman is a more common way nowadays for exchanging session keys.
Tiffy Helman is complicated, but in a nutshell, it uses some advanced math involving large prime numbers
to derive a share session key without ever transmitting a public key over the network.
Well, that is it for HTTPS.
You would like to learn more about system design, check out our books and weekly newsletter.
Please subscribe if you learned something new.
Thank you so much and we'll see you next time.
